A new eval config, `configs/eval-config-time-to-mock.json`, measures how fast and how cheaply the agent gets a styled mockup in front of the client. Each of its three cases opens with a short, style-bearing ask and a goal-holding client that wants to look at the mockup before anything is built for real, and stops the moment the agent says the mockup is ready to look at and where to find it. The client never insists that the agent opens anything for it: a headless workspace has no connected frontend, so a tab cannot be opened. The client never approves the design, so the template's confirmation gate keeps the hardening pass and its background worker from ever starting.

Every trial now records each client turn: `state.json` and the trial metadata carry a `turns` list with when the message was sent, when its reply was complete, how long that took, and the tokens and cost the workspace agent spent answering it, plus `conversation_seconds` from the first send to the last reply. `usage.json` carries the same records as `per_turn`. Per-turn usage is read from the transcript, so it carries the transcript's caveats: no delegated or worker spend, standard-rate pricing, and a null cost on a codex trial. It is a floor on what the trial spent rather than a partition of it -- the welcome turn is before the first record, and the workspace's turn-end flow can spend past the poll that closed a turn -- so the per-turn figures do not sum to the trial's totals. Nothing at grade time reads these; they are observability in the artifacts, for cases whose question is "how long until the mock" rather than "was the app delivered".

A case's `expectations` may declare a `process` block: `required_skills` the agent must invoke, `forbidden_skills` it must not, and `max_worker_launches`. The evidence phase reads the captured common transcript for skill invocations (a `Skill` tool call on claude, a read or shell command naming `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` on the other harnesses) and for background-worker launches, and records one `process` manifest entry per check. A call whose result came back an error invoked nothing: a `Skill` call answered `Unknown skill` never ran the skill, and a command that failed never opened its file. The verifier scores them as `process_expectations_met` in the outcome dimension. A trial whose transcript could not be captured, or whose transcript came out holding no record of the agent, records every process entry as an error, which errors the trial rather than scoring it, since the instrument failed rather than the agent.

A case's `expectations` may also declare a `timing` block, which turns latency into part of the score rather than only an observation: `fast_seconds`, `slow_seconds`, and an optional `requires_no_failures`. It measures the wall-clock from the case's first client message to the reply that satisfied a goal entry's client, and scores it clamped and linear in log time -- `score = clamp((ln slow - ln t) / (ln slow - ln fast), 0, 1)` -- so a trial at or under `fast_seconds` scores 1.0, one at or over `slow_seconds` scores 0.0, and the per-case anchors stay comparable across cases because the curve is scale-free. The verifier scores it as `time_to_goal_within_expectations` in the outcome dimension. `requires_no_failures` names expectation classes whose failure zeroes the time outright, since being fast at something other than what the case commissioned is not what the class measures; the manifest entry records which prerequisite zeroed it, alongside the seconds it measured, so a fast trial that scored nothing says why. A client that was never satisfied is unbounded time and scores 0.0 rather than erroring the trial: it is a measurement of the agent, not a broken instrument.

To support it, every entry in `state.json` now carries `satisfied_at` and `satisfied_at_turn`, naming the reply the goal-holding client ruled on. The client judges the conversation as it stands, so that reply is frequently not one of the entry's own exchanges -- a goal already met by the previous entry's reply sends nothing and records `exchange_count: 0` -- and the outcome labels alone could not say when the goal was met. Manifest entries carry an optional `value` for a class that scores a continuous measurement.

The three `configs/eval-config-time-to-mock.json` cases now declare `timing` with `requires_no_failures: ["app"]`: todo-mock 150/600 s, habit-tracker-mock 220/880 s, recipe-box-mock 500/2000 s. Those anchors are provisional, calibrated from a five-trial-per-cell A/B, and are to be re-set from the first clean nightly. Their goal text is also tighter about what counts as being told where to look: a named tab, app name or file path in the agent's reply is explicitly enough, and the client does not ask again. It still never demands that a tab be opened, and still never approves the design.

`configs/nightly_suites.json` is the new checked-in list of **suites**: one eval config plus the harness configs worth running it on. It is the single place that names what a night costs, and the nightly evaluates every suite against both frozen pairs. The `eval-config-small.json` suite names no arms, which means every entry `configs/harness_configs.json` marks `is_nightly` -- exactly the cells that ran before -- and the `eval-config-time-to-mock.json` suite names `opus-standard`, `codex-sol-low` and `codex-terra`, whatever their nightly flag says. So `opus-standard` now runs nightly against time-to-mock and against nothing else.

An arm may carry `attempts`, a positive whole number that becomes harbor's `-k`, for a measurement one sample is too noisy to read. It defaults to 1, no `-k` is passed at that count, the cell's concurrency is its case count times its attempts so every trial still runs in one wave, and the count is deliberately not part of a green marker key.

`minds-evals ci-matrix` composes the run's cells across suites, pairs and arms and validates the suite file on the free `resolve` job: repo-relative `.json` configs that are in the checkout, arm names `harness_configs.json` holds, positive attempts, no config named twice, and no two configs whose file names shorten to one **config slug**. Its `--config` option is now optional -- it names one ad-hoc suite instead of the list -- and `--select` overrides the arms of every suite the run evaluates. Every cell carries its own config, config slug and attempts.

The oracle pass runs per (pair, eval config) rather than per pair: it exercises the generated task, the verifier container and grading, all of which are the eval config's own, and each cell gates on the oracle of its own config. Every job name, concurrency group, harbor job name, artifact name and summary file name carries the config slug (`main-eval-config-time-to-mock-codex-terra`), so two suites cannot overwrite each other's names or summaries; `oracle` stays a reserved harness config name, which is what keeps an oracle pass's artifacts apart from its suite's cells'.

`minds-evals ci-report` posts one Slack message per pair and eval config, each with its own oracle verdict, grid and judge table -- a config's cases and arms are its own. A pair the run skipped whole or could not resolve still gets a single message, and a suite whose every cell is already green reads as skipped rather than as missing its oracle.
